claims.source: Further, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EHD2 knockout (KO) in TNBC cell lines (Figure 5A), which unlike our observations in Ehd2-KO mouse tissues was not associated with any significant changes in EHD1/4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), significantly impaired their migration, invasion (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), another pro-metastatic trait (Cheung and Ewald, 2014).
claims.evidence: Immunoblot analysis showed no significant changes in EHD1/4 expression in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: EHD2 knockout significantly impaired migration and invasion of TNBC cells.
claims.source: Further, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EHD2 knockout (KO) in TNBC cell lines (Figure 5A), which unlike our observations in Ehd2-KO mouse tissues was not associated with any significant changes in EHD1/4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), significantly impaired their migration, invasion (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), another pro-metastatic trait (Cheung and Ewald, 2014).
claims.evidence: Transwell migration and invasion assays showed significant impairment with EHD2 knockout (Figure 5B-C).

claims.claim: EHD2 knockout significantly impaired extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability of TNBC cells.
claims.source: Further, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EHD2 knockout (KO) in TNBC cell lines (Figure 5A), which unlike our observations in Ehd2-KO mouse tissues was not associated with any significant changes in EHD1/4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), significantly impaired their migration, invasion (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), another pro-metastatic trait (Cheung and Ewald, 2014).
claims.evidence: ECM degradation assay showed significant reduction with EHD2 knockout (Figure 5D), with citation to Cheung and Ewald, 2014 for ECM degradation as a pro-metastatic trait.

claims.claim: Introduction of mouse Ehd2 in MDA-MB-231 EHD2-KO cells significantly rescued the cell migration defect.
claims.source: Introduction of mouse Ehd2 in MDA-MB-231 EHD2-KO cells, at levels lower than in control cells, significantly rescued the cell migration defect (Figure 5E), demonstrating specificity.
claims.evidence: Mouse Ehd2 rescue experiment showed significant rescue of migration defect (Figure 5E).

claims.claim: CRISPR activation of endogenous EHD2 in EHD2-nonexpressing MDA-MB-468 TNBC cells increased cell migration compared to control cells.
claims.source: Reciprocally, CRISPR activation of endogenous EHD2 in EHD2-nonexpressing MDA-MB-468 TNBC cells (Figure 5F) increased cell migration compared to control cells (Figure 5G).
claims.evidence: CRISPRa induction of EHD2 in MDA-MB-468 cells increased migration (Figure 5F-G).

claims.claim: EHD2-KO MDA-MB-231 cells exhibited a marked and significant defect in orthotopic tumor formation, with significant rescue upon mouse Ehd2 expression.
claims.source: When orthotopically implanted in nude mice, EHD2-KO MDA-MB-231 cells exhibited a marked and significant defect in tumor formation, with a significant rescue upon mouse Ehd2 expression (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: Xenograft tumorigenesis assay showed marked defect in EHD2-KO cells with rescue by mouse Ehd2 (Figure 5H).

claims.claim: Intravenously injected control MDA-MB-231 cells showed time-dependent lung metastatic growth while EHD2-KO cells showed no growth or reduction in signals.
claims.source: Luminescence bioimaging showed time-dependent lung metastatic growth of control cells but no growth (or a reduction in signals) with EHD2-KO cells (Figure 6A–C).
claims.evidence: Bioluminescence imaging showed lung metastatic growth in control but not EHD2-KO cells (Figure 6A-C).

claims.claim: EHD2-KO MDA-MB-231 cells showed nearly complete absence of metastatic nodules in lungs at necropsy.
claims.source: These findings were confirmed by assessment of lung metastatic nodules at necropsy (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Quantification of tumor nodules in lungs showed nearly complete absence in EHD2-KO group (Figure 6D).

claims.claim: EHD2 and CAV1 mRNAs show tight co-expression in TNBC samples.
claims.source: The bc-GenExMiner analysis of 5277 BC samples Jézéquel et al., 2013 demonstrated tight co-expression of EHD2 with the structural components of caveolae, CAV1 and CAV2 in TNBC samples (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: bc-GenExMiner analysis showed Pearson's correlation of R=0.7 for EHD2/CAV1 in TNBC (Figure 7A), with citation to Jézéquel et al., 2013.

claims.claim: EHD2 and CAV2 mRNAs show tight co-expression in TNBC samples.
claims.source: The bc-GenExMiner analysis of 5277 BC samples Jézéquel et al., 2013 demonstrated tight co-expression of EHD2 with the structural components of caveolae, CAV1 and CAV2 in TNBC samples (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: bc-GenExMiner analysis showed Pearson's correlation of R=0.51 for EHD2/CAV2 in TNBC (Figure 7A), with citation to Jézéquel et al., 2013.

claims.claim: Combined EHD2-, CAV1-, and CAV2-high basal BC patients showed significantly shorter distal metastasis-free survival.
claims.source: By KM Plotter analysis, combined EHD2-, CAV1-, and CAV2-high basal (PAM50-based) but not all BC patients showed significantly shorter distal metastasis-free survival (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: KM Plotter analysis showed shorter relapse-free survival in basal-like BC with high EHD2, CAV1, and CAV2 (Figure 7B).

claims.claim: EHD2 and CAV1 show concordant expression in mammary epithelial and breast cancer cell lines.
claims.source: Immunoblotting demonstrated concordant EHD2 and CAV1 expression in mammary epithelial and BC cell lines (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting showed coordinate EHD2 and CAV1 expression across cell lines (Figure 7C).

claims.claim: EHD2 and CAV1 show a high degree of colocalization in TNBC cell lines.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence analysis using structured illumination microscopy (SIM) demonstrated a high degree of colocalization between EHD2 and CAV1 in TNBC cell lines (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: SIM images showed colocalization of EHD2 and CAV1 with Pearson's Coefficient of Colocalization around 0.6-0.7 (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: EHD2-KO cells show a significant reduction of cell surface associated CAV1-GFP puncta (caveolae).
claims.source: Total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy analysis showed a significant reduction of cell surface associated CAV1-GFP puncta, representing cell surface caveolae, in EHD2-KO compared to control Hs578T cells (Figure 7E), consistent with the reported electron microcopy-based high cell surface caveolae density on Hs578T compared to a lower density on the EHD2-non-expressing MDA-MB-436 cells (Torrino et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: TIRF microscopy showed significant reduction in CAV1 puncta per cell in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 7E), consistent with citation to Torrino et al., 2018.

claims.claim: CAV1 knockout led to significant impairment of cell migration in TNBC cells.
claims.source: CRISPR KO of CAV1 (Figure 7F) led to a significant impairment of cell migration like that with EHD2-KO (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: Transwell migration assay showed significant reduction with CAV1-KO (Figure 7G).

claims.claim: EHD2-dependent maintenance of cell surface caveolae is linked to its promotion of tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits.
claims.source: These results support the conclusion that EHD2-dependent maintenance of cell surface caveolae is linked to its promotion of tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits, although the potential role(s) of EHD2 and caveolae in other subcellular locations cannot be excluded at present.
claims.evidence: Based on co-expression, colocalization, and functional effects of EHD2 and CAV1 knockout (Figure 7).

claims.claim: Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) operates at caveolae.
claims.source: We investigated the linkage of EHD2 to store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) (Chung et al., 2017), a pathway that operates at caveolae (Pani and Singh, 2009; Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017) and is a well-established pro-metastatic signaling pathway in TNBC and other cancers (Mo and Yang, 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Pani and Singh, 2009 and Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017.

claims.claim: SOCE is a well-established pro-metastatic signaling pathway in TNBC and other cancers.
claims.source: We investigated the linkage of EHD2 to store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) (Chung et al., 2017), a pathway that operates at caveolae (Pani and Singh, 2009; Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017) and is a well-established pro-metastatic signaling pathway in TNBC and other cancers (Mo and Yang, 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Mo and Yang, 2018 and Yang et al., 2009.

claims.claim: SOCE is mediated by translocation of ER Ca2+ sensor STIM1 to ER-plasma membrane contact sites upon ER Ca2+ depletion.
claims.source: The SOCE is mediated by translocation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ sensor stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) to ER-plasma membrane contact sites upon ER Ca2+ depletion which permits its binding to and activation of the Orai1 membrane Ca2+ channel to promote Ca2+ entry for Ca2+-dependent signaling and refilling of the ER (Chung et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claims.claim: STIM1 binding to and activation of Orai1 membrane Ca2+ channel promotes Ca2+ entry for Ca2+-dependent signaling and refilling of the ER.
claims.source: The SOCE is mediated by translocation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ sensor stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) to ER-plasma membrane contact sites upon ER Ca2+ depletion which permits its binding to and activation of the Orai1 membrane Ca2+ channel to promote Ca2+ entry for Ca2+-dependent signaling and refilling of the ER (Chung et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Control TNBC cells exhibited a robust rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ upon thapsigargin treatment in Ca2+-free medium.
claims.source: Expectedly, control Hs578T or BT549 TNBC cells exhibited a robust rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ that declined over time (Figure 8A–B), reflecting the release of ER Ca2+ (Ong et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Fluo4-AM loaded cells showed robust Ca2+ rise upon thapsigargin treatment (Figure 8A-B), with citation to Ong et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Addition of Ca2+ in the medium after thapsigargin treatment induced a rapid increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+, indicating SOCE.
claims.source: Subsequent addition of Ca2+ in the medium induced a rapid increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+, indicating the SOCE (Figure 8A–B; Ong et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assay showed rapid increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+ upon Ca2+ addition (Figure 8A-B), with citation to Ong et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Pre-treatment with SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 markedly reduced the initial Ca2+ flux and nearly abrogated the SOCE.
claims.source: Pre-treatment with the SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 (Yang et al., 2009) markedly reduced the initial Ca2+ flux and nearly abrogated the SOCE (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assay with SKF96365 pre-treatment showed marked reduction in both phases (Figure 8C), with citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claims.claim: EHD2-KO cells demonstrated a marked defect in both the initial Tg-induced rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ and the subsequent SOCE.
claims.source: EHD2-KO cells demonstrated a marked defect in both the initial Tg-induced rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ and the subsequent SOCE (Figure 8A–B), consistent with the established role of SOCE in intracellular Ca2+ store filling (the source of the initial Ca2+ release upon Tg treatment) besides Ca2+-dependent signaling (Chung et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assays showed marked defects in both phases in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8A-B), with citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Defective SOCE was observed in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells using cyclopiazonic acid (CPA).
claims.source: Defective SOCE was also seen in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells using another SERCA inhibitor cyclopiazonic acid (CPA) (Demaurex et al., 1992; Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assay with CPA showed defective SOCE in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8D), with citation to Demaurex et al., 1992.

claims.claim: EHD2-KO Hs578T cells expressing GCaMP6s exhibited defective Tg-induced SOCE.
claims.source: In a genetic approach, we showed that EHD2-KO Hs578T cells stably expressing a GFP-based reporter of cytoplasmic Ca2+, GCaMP6s, (Chen et al., 2013), exhibited defective Tg-induced SOCE (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assay using GCaMP6s reporter showed defective SOCE in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8E), with citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: EHD2-KO Hs578T cells expressing GCaMP6s-CAAX showed defective SOCE.
claims.source: Further, stable expression of GCaMP6s-CAAX, a plasma membrane-targeted fluorescent reporter of Ca2+ levels (Tsai et al., 2014), which only detects the SOCE phase upon Tg treatment directly established the defective SOCE in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assay using GCaMP6s-CAAX reporter showed defective SOCE in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8F), with citation to Tsai et al., 2014.

claims.claim: CRISPRa-induced endogenous EHD2 expression in EHD2-negative MDA-MB-468 cells led to a marked increase in Tg-induced SOCE.
claims.source: In a reciprocal experiment, CRISPRa- induced endogenous EHD2 expression in EHD2-negative MDA-MB-468 cells led to a marked increase in Tg-induced SOCE (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assay showed marked increase in SOCE with CRISPRa-induced EHD2 expression (Figure 8G).

claims.claim: A marked defect in SOCE was observed in CAV1-KO TNBC cell lines.
claims.source: Consistent with the role of caveolae, a marked defect in SOCE was observed in CAV1-KO TNBC cell lines (Figure 8H–I).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assays showed marked defects in SOCE in CAV1-KO cells (Figure 8H-I).

claims.claim: Thapsigargin treatment failed to increase STIM1 puncta at the cell surface in EHD2-KO cells.
claims.source: Tg treatment failed to increase the STIM1 puncta in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: TIRF microscopy showed no increase in STIM1 puncta with thapsigargin treatment in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9A).

claims.claim: The defect in STIM1 puncta formation in EHD2-KO cells was not a result of reduced levels of total STIM1 and Orai1 proteins.
claims.source: This defect was not a result of reduced levels of total STIM1 and Orai1 proteins (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: Immunoblotting showed comparable total STIM1 and Orai1 levels in control vs EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9B).

claims.claim: Orai1 localizes in caveolae.
claims.source: Given the known localization of Orai1 in caveolae (Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017; Sathish et al., 2012), we assessed the impact of EHD2-KO on Orai1 cell surface levels.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017 and Sathish et al., 2012.

claims.claim: EHD2-KO cells showed a marked reduction in cell surface Orai1 levels.
claims.source: In contrast, streptavidin blotting revealed a marked reduction in biotinylated (cell surface) Orai1 signals in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9C, upper panels).
claims.evidence: Cell surface biotinylation followed by Orai1 immunoprecipitation showed marked reduction in surface Orai1 in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9C).

claims.claim: Overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells partially rescued the SOCE defect.
claims.source: Further linking the SOCE to EHD2-dependent pro-metastatic traits, overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells (Figure 9D) partially rescued the SOCE defect (Figure 9E) and the defective cell migration (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: Ca2+ flux assay showed partial rescue of SOCE with STIM1 overexpression (Figure 9E).

claims.claim: Overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells partially rescued the defective cell migration.
claims.source: Further linking the SOCE to EHD2-dependent pro-metastatic traits, overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells (Figure 9D) partially rescued the SOCE defect (Figure 9E) and the defective cell migration (Figure 9F).
claims.evidence: Transwell migration assay showed partial rescue with STIM1 overexpression (Figure 9F).

claims.claim: SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 significantly impaired wildtype TNBC cell migration.
claims.source: In a complementary approach, the tool SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 and a recently identified inhibitor CM4620, which (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions (Bruen et al., 2022), significantly impaired the wildtype TNBC cell migration, and further reduced the migration of EHD2-KO cells, albeit the latter was not statistically significant (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: Transwell migration assay with SKF96365 showed significant reduction in wildtype TNBC cell migration (Figure 10A), with citation to Bruen et al., 2022 for CM4620.

claims.claim: SOCE inhibitor CM4620 significantly impaired wildtype TNBC cell migration.
claims.source: In a complementary approach, the tool SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 and a recently identified inhibitor CM4620, which (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions (Bruen et al., 2022), significantly impaired the wildtype TNBC cell migration, and further reduced the migration of EHD2-KO cells, albeit the latter was not statistically significant (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: Transwell migration assay with CM4620 showed significant reduction in wildtype TNBC cell migration (Figure 10A), with citation to Bruen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: CM4620 (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions.
claims.source: In a complementary approach, the tool SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 and a recently identified inhibitor CM4620, which (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions (Bruen et al., 2022), significantly impaired the wildtype TNBC cell migration, and further reduced the migration of EHD2-KO cells, albeit the latter was not statistically significant (Figure 10A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Bruen et al., 2022.

claims.claim: A major proportion of the SOCE in TNBC cell lines is dependent on EHD2 and is inhibitable with available SOCE inhibitors.
claims.source: Thus, a major proportion of the SOCE in TNBC cell lines is dependent on EHD2 and is inhibitable with available SOCE inhibitors.
claims.evidence: Based on marked defects in SOCE with EHD2-KO (Figure 8) and significant inhibition with SKF96365 and CM4620 (Figure 10A).

claims.claim: SKF96365 treatment significantly reduced control TNBC xenograft tumor growth.
claims.source: Accordingly, we show that SKF96365 treatment significantly reduced the control TNBC xenograft tumor growth (Figure 10B); we were unable to test the SOCE inhibitor against EHD2-KO TNBC xenografts as these did not grow sufficiently to test the inhibitor impact.
claims.evidence: Xenograft tumor growth assay showed significant reduction with SKF96365 treatment (Figure 10B).

claims.claim: EHD2, by stabilizing caveolae, facilitates SOCE to promote downstream pro-oncogenic traits in TNBC cells.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings support our conclusion that EHD2, by stabilizing caveolae, facilitates the SOCE to promote downstream pro-oncogenic traits in TNBC cells.
claims.evidence: Based on collective findings showing EHD2 stabilizes caveolae (Figure 7E), regulates SOCE (Figure 8-9), and promotes oncogenic traits (Figure 4-6).

claims.claim: High cytoplasmic EHD2 expression was found in a substantial proportion of breast tumors.
claims.source: Our IHC analyses demonstrated high cytoplasmic EHD2 expression in a substantial proportion of breast tumors, associated with shorter BC-specific patient survival (Figure 3B) and higher tumor grade (Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
claims.evidence: IHC analysis of 840 BC samples showed high cytoplasmic EHD2 in substantial proportion (Figure 3).

claims.claim: A higher proportion of TNBC, luminal B and HER2+ patients exhibited high cytoplasmic EHD2.
claims.source: A higher proportion of TNBC, luminal B and HER2 + patients exhibited high cytoplasmic EHD2 (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
claims.evidence: Analysis of IHC data across BC subtypes showed this distribution (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).

claims.claim: Previous studies reported reduction in EHD2 expression correlates with tumor progression in breast cancer.
claims.source: Our results differ from reports that reduction in EHD2 expression correlates with tumor progression in BC (Yang et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2015 and Shi et al., 2015.

claims.claim: High EHD2 expression in normal mammary adipocytes could result in apparent reduction in EHD2 expression in tumor tissue using western blotting.
claims.source: Several factors could account for the discordance, including the lack of validation of antibodies in prior studies, the high EHD2 expression in normal mammary adipocytes (Figure 1B), resulting in apparent reduction in EHD2 expression in tumor tissue using western blotting (Yang et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2015), and the possibility that EHD2 signals in prior studies represented nuclear EHD2, which we find is associated with positive prognostic factors (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
claims.evidence: Inferred from high adipocyte EHD2 expression (Figure 1B) and discordance with prior western blot studies.

claims.claim: EHD2 signals in prior studies may have represented nuclear EHD2, which is associated with positive prognostic factors.
claims.source: Several factors could account for the discordance, including the lack of validation of antibodies in prior studies, the high EHD2 expression in normal mammary adipocytes (Figure 1B), resulting in apparent reduction in EHD2 expression in tumor tissue using western blotting (Yang et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2015), and the possibility that EHD2 signals in prior studies represented nuclear EHD2, which we find is associated with positive prognostic factors (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
claims.evidence: Inferred from finding that nuclear EHD2 is associated with positive prognosis (Figure 3B) and prior studies did not distinguish nuclear vs cytoplasmic EHD2.

claims.claim: EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals.
claims.source: Previous cell-line-based studies have shown that EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals, the latter dependent on its SUMOylation, and that nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains (Pekar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pekar et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Nuclear EHD2 exit is dependent on its SUMOylation.
claims.source: Previous cell-line-based studies have shown that EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals, the latter dependent on its SUMOylation, and that nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains (Pekar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pekar et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains.
claims.source: Previous cell-line-based studies have shown that EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals, the latter dependent on its SUMOylation, and that nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains (Pekar et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Pekar et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Application of mechanical stress to cells led to EHD2 release from caveolae, its SUMOylation and nuclear translocation where it regulated transcription of several genes including caveolar components.
claims.source: Another study found that application of mechanical stress to cells led to EHD2 release from caveolae, its SUMOylation and nuclear translocation where it regulated transcription of several genes including caveolar components, in a potential positive feedback mechanism (Torrino et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Torrino et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Nuclear translocation of EHD2 may sequester EHD2 to inhibit its plasma membrane-associated pro-oncogenic role in SOCE.
claims.source: In view of the opposite prognostic significance of nuclear vs. non-nuclear EHD2 in our analyses of BC patient samples, it could be speculated that nuclear translocation may sequester EHD2 to inhibit its plasma membrane-associated pro-oncogenic role in SOCE, but rigorous studies will be needed to test this suggestion.
claims.evidence: Speculated based on opposite prognostic significance of nuclear vs cytoplasmic EHD2 (Figure 3B).

claims.claim: EHD2 is required for tumorigenesis under stringent conditions (tumorspheres).
claims.source: We show that in vitro tumor cell growth under stringent conditions (tumorspheres; Figure 4C) and pro-metastatic traits of cell migration, invasion, and ECM degradation (Figures 4D–E–5B–D) are EHD2-dependent.
claims.evidence: Tumorsphere assay showed EHD2 knockdown markedly reduced tumorsphere growth (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: Pro-metastatic traits of cell migration, invasion, and ECM degradation are EHD2-dependent.
claims.source: We show that in vitro tumor cell growth under stringent conditions (tumorspheres; Figure 4C) and pro-metastatic traits of cell migration, invasion, and ECM degradation (Figures 4D–E–5B–D) are EHD2-dependent.
claims.evidence: Multiple assays showed EHD2 knockdown or knockout impaired migration, invasion, and ECM degradation (Figures 4D-E, 5B-D).

claims.claim: Extranuclear EHD2 overexpression in breast cancer cells represents a key pro-tumorigenic and pro-metastatic adaptation.
claims.source: Although further studies are needed to fully dissect the steps at which EHD2 is critical in the metastatic process, collectively, our analyses conclusively demonstrate that extranuclear EHD2 overexpression in BC cells represents a key pro-tumorigenic and pro-metastatic adaptation.
claims.evidence: Based on collective in vitro and in vivo data showing EHD2 promotes tumorigenesis and metastasis (Figures 4-6).

claims.claim: EHD2 stabilizes caveolae.
claims.source: Mechanistically, we link the EHD2 overexpression in BC cells to regulation of caveolae, whose stability is known to be controlled by EHD2 (Morén et al., 2012; Stoeber et al., 2012; Morén et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Morén et al., 2012; Stoeber et al., 2012; Morén et al., 2019, and TIRF data showing reduced caveolae in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 7E).

claims.claim: CAV1 has pro-tumorigenic roles in TNBC.
claims.source: This includes the strong EHD2 co-localization with CAV1/2 (Figure 7D), reduction in cell surface caveolae density using TIRF microscopy upon EHD2-KO (Figure 7E), and inhibition of TNBC cell migration upon CAV1-KO (Figure 7G), consistent with the previously documented pro-tumorigenic roles of CAV1 in TNBC (Badana et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Badana et al., 2016 and Zou et al., 2017.

claims.claim: CAV1 localizes in various intracellular locations besides the plasma membrane.
claims.source: However, since our localization analyses show both EHD2 and CAV1 to also localize intracellularly besides at the plasma membrane (Figure 7D), and prior studies have identified pro-oncogenic roles for CAV1 localized in various intracellular locations (Simón et al., 2020), further studies will be needed to determine if the role of EHD2 we define here is exclusively related to regulation of the plasma membrane caveolae or might involve CAV1 in other compartments as well.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Simón et al., 2020 and SIM images showing intracellular localization (Figure 7D).

claims.claim: Caveolae serve as hubs for signaling.
claims.source: Caveolae serve as hubs for signaling (Lamaze et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Lamaze et al., 2017.

claims.claim: SOCE pathway regulates multiple tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits in TNBC.
claims.source: Among these, the SOCE pathway stood out as it is known to regulate multiple tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits in TNBC (Pani and Singh, 2009; Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017), as with EHD2 depletion.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Pani and Singh, 2009 and Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017.

claims.claim: EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins.
claims.source: Also, EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins (Posey et al., 2011) that are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair and EHD2 was found to accumulate at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models (Marg et al., 2012; Demonbreun et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Posey et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Ferlins are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair.
claims.source: Also, EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins (Posey et al., 2011) that are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair and EHD2 was found to accumulate at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models (Marg et al., 2012; Demonbreun et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Posey et al., 2011.

claims.claim: EHD2 accumulates at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models.
claims.source: Also, EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins (Posey et al., 2011) that are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair and EHD2 was found to accumulate at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models (Marg et al., 2012; Demonbreun et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Marg et al., 2012 and Demonbreun et al., 2016.

claims.claim: EHD2 is a major positive regulator of SOCE in TNBC cell models.
claims.source: Indeed, our extensive analyses demonstrate that EHD2 is a major positive regulator of SOCE in TNBC cell models.
claims.evidence: Based on multiple Ca2+ flux assays showing marked defects in SOCE with EHD2-KO and increases with EHD2 overexpression (Figure 8).

claims.claim: SOCE plays a role in intracellular Ca2+ store refilling.
claims.source: Consistent with the established role of SOCE in the intracellular Ca2+ store refilling (Chung et al., 2017), which then serves as the source of the initial Ca2+ release upon appropriate stimuli (Tg or CPA in our studies), loss of EHD2 or CAV1 expression or treatment with SOCE inhibitors led to an impairment of the SOCE as well as the initial Ca2+ peak (Figure 8A–E; Figure 8H–I).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017 and Ca2+ flux data (Figure 8).

claims.claim: Orai1 is a major STIM1-interacting caveolae-resident SOCE channel.
claims.source: Orai1 is a major STIM1-interacting caveolae-resident SOCE channel (Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017; Sathish et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017 and Sathish et al., 2012.

claims.claim: EHD2-dependent stabilization of cell surface caveolae ensures high cell surface levels of Orai1 to enable robust SOCE in TNBCs.
claims.source: Thus, our findings support a model whereby EHD2-dependent stabilization of cell surface caveolae ensures high cell surface levels of Orai1 to enable robust SOCE in TNBCs, which in turn promotes pro-tumorigenic and pro-metastatic behaviors of tumor cells (Mo and Yang, 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Based on findings that EHD2-KO reduces cell surface caveolae (Figure 7E), reduces cell surface Orai1 (Figure 9C), and impairs SOCE (Figure 8), with citations to Mo and Yang, 2018 and Yang et al., 2009.

claims.claim: EHD2 deficiency reduced the cell surface levels of caveolae-associated ATP-sensitive K+ channels.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, EHD2 deficiency reduced the cell surface levels of caveolae-associated ATP-sensitive K+ channels (Yang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Chemical inhibition of SOCE markedly impaired the pro-metastatic traits of EHD2-overexpressing TNBCs.
claims.source: Finally, consistent with prior studies (Yang et al., 2009), chemical inhibition of SOCE markedly impaired the pro-metastatic traits of EHD2-overexpressing TNBCs, with a smaller impact on EHD2-KO cell lines (Figure 10A) and impaired the TNBC metastatic growth in vivo (Figure 10B).
claims.evidence: SOCE inhibitors significantly reduced migration of wildtype TNBC cells (Figure 10A) and tumor growth in vivo (Figure 10B), with citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claims.claim: SKF96365 targets additional Ca2+ channels besides Orai1.
claims.source: However, since SKF96365 targets additional Ca2+ channels besides Orai1 (Ramsey et al., 2006; Ding et al., 2012), further studies using more selective inhibitors together with genetic analyses will be needed.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ramsey et al., 2006 and Ding et al., 2012.

claims.claim: EHD2-overexpressing subsets of TNBC and other BC subtypes may be selectively amenable to SOCE targeting.
claims.source: Together, our studies support the idea that EHD2-overexpressing subsets of TNBC and other BC subtypes may be selectively amenable to SOCE targeting, with EHD2 and CAV1/2 overexpression as predictors of response.
claims.evidence: Based on findings that EHD2 regulates SOCE (Figure 8-9), SOCE inhibitors impair TNBC cell migration and tumor growth (Figure 10), and EHD2/CAV1/2 co-overexpression predicts poor survival (Figure 7B).

claims.claim: EHD2 and CAV1/2 overexpression may serve as predictors of response to SOCE targeting.
claims.source: Together, our studies support the idea that EHD2-overexpressing subsets of TNBC and other BC subtypes may be selectively amenable to SOCE targeting, with EHD2 and CAV1/2 overexpression as predictors of response.
claims.evidence: Based on co-expression of EHD2 and CAV1/2 (Figure 7A), their association with poor survival (Figure 7B), and role in SOCE (Figure 8).

results.result: EHD2 is selectively expressed in basal mammary epithelial cells and a subset of basal-like/TNBC cell lines, particularly those of mesenchymal subtype, with predominantly cytoplasmic/membrane localization.
results.evaluation: Multiple complementary methods (immunofluorescence, IHC, immunoblotting) consistently demonstrate basal cell-selective EHD2 expression in mouse mammary gland (C28, C30) and correlation with TNBC mesenchymal subtype in cell lines (C32, C37). Protein expression patterns correlate with mRNA data from CCLE database (C36), providing independent validation. The exclusive cytoplasmic/membrane localization (C35) is consistently observed across methods.

results.result: High cytoplasmic EHD2 expression in breast cancer patient samples is associated with aggressive tumor features and shorter survival, particularly in TNBC and basal-like subtypes, while nuclear EHD2 shows opposite prognostic associations.
results.evaluation: Large patient cohort (759-756 valid cases from 840 samples; C39, C40) with rigorous IHC analysis distinguishing cytoplasmic vs. nuclear localization provides strong statistical power. High cytoplasmic EHD2 correlates with higher grade, mitosis, and shorter survival (C41, C43, C48), while nuclear EHD2 shows opposite associations (C42, C44, C47). The subcellular localization-dependent prognostic differences are novel and well-documented, though the biological basis requires further investigation.

results.result: EHD2, CAV1, and CAV2 mRNAs show tight co-expression in TNBC samples, and their combined overexpression predicts shorter survival specifically in basal-like breast cancer.
results.evaluation: Large-scale mRNA analysis (5277 BC samples) demonstrates strong Pearson correlations (R=0.7 for EHD2/CAV1, R=0.51 for EHD2/CAV2; C64, C65) in TNBC. KM Plotter analysis of combined high expression shows significantly shorter survival in basal-like BC (C66, C4), with specificity for this subtype. The co-expression pattern supports a functional relationship, though causality requires experimental validation.

results.result: EHD2 shRNA knockdown in TNBC cell lines impairs tumorsphere growth, invasion, ECM degradation, and xenograft tumor formation without affecting 2D proliferation on plastic.
results.evaluation: Multiple TNBC cell lines tested with consistent phenotypes across diverse assays (tumorspheres, transwell invasion, 3D organoid invasion, xenografts; C50-C53). The lack of effect on 2D proliferation (C49) but strong effects on 3D growth and invasion suggests EHD2 specifically regulates tumor-relevant phenotypes. Xenograft data show marked reduction in tumor volume and Ki67+ proliferation (C53, C54), with reduced metastasis in MDA-MB-231 (C55). However, shRNA approaches have potential off-target effects.

results.result: CRISPR-Cas9 EHD2 knockout with mouse Ehd2 rescue definitively establishes EHD2 as essential for TNBC tumorigenesis and metastasis, regulating migration, invasion, ECM degradation, and metastatic colonization.
results.evaluation: CRISPR-Cas9 knockout provides more specific genetic perturbation than shRNA, with no compensatory changes in EHD1/4 (C56). Multiple TNBC lines show consistent impairment of migration, invasion, and ECM degradation (C57, C58). Critical rescue experiment with mouse Ehd2 (C59) demonstrates specificity. Reciprocal CRISPRa experiment increasing EHD2 enhances migration (C60). In vivo, EHD2-KO severely impairs orthotopic tumor formation with rescue by mouse Ehd2 (C61), and completely blocks lung metastasis after IV injection (C62, C63). The convergence of loss-of-function, rescue, and gain-of-function data provides strong causal evidence.

results.result: EHD2 stabilizes cell surface caveolae through colocalization with CAV1, and both EHD2 and CAV1 knockout impair TNBC cell migration, linking caveolae stability to pro-metastatic traits.
results.evaluation: Concordant protein expression (C67), high-resolution SIM showing colocalization (Pearson coefficient ~0.6-0.7; C68), and TIRF microscopy demonstrating reduced surface caveolae in EHD2-KO cells (C69) provide strong evidence for EHD2-caveolae relationship. Functional validation through CAV1-KO showing similar migration defects as EHD2-KO (C70) supports shared pathway. However, both proteins also localize intracellularly (acknowledged in manuscript), so exclusive plasma membrane mechanism remains uncertain. The conclusion (C71, C110) is well-supported but appropriately cautious about other potential roles.

results.result: EHD2 is a major positive regulator of store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) in TNBC cells, with EHD2 knockout markedly impairing both ER Ca2+ release and SOCE phases.
results.evaluation: Extensive Ca2+ flux measurements using multiple approaches: fluorescent dye (Fluo4-AM; C76-C80), genetic reporters (GCaMP6s cytoplasmic and GCaMP6s-CAAX membrane-targeted; C81, C82), two different SERCA inhibitors (thapsigargin and CPA; C79, C80), and multiple cell lines. EHD2-KO consistently shows marked defects in both ER release and SOCE phases. Reciprocal CRISPRa experiment shows increased SOCE with EHD2 induction (C83). CAV1-KO shows similar SOCE defects (C84), supporting caveolae-dependent mechanism. The convergence of multiple independent methods and bidirectional perturbations provides robust evidence.

results.result: EHD2 regulates SOCE by maintaining high cell surface levels of Orai1 through caveolae stabilization, with reduced surface Orai1 and impaired STIM1 puncta formation in EHD2-KO cells, and partial rescue by STIM1 overexpression.
results.evaluation: Cell surface biotinylation shows marked reduction in surface Orai1 in EHD2-KO cells despite normal total protein levels (C88, C86). TIRF microscopy demonstrates failure of STIM1 puncta formation upon thapsigargin treatment in EHD2-KO cells (C85). STIM1 overexpression partially rescues both SOCE and migration defects (C89, C90), supporting the proposed mechanism. The model linking EHD2→caveolae→surface Orai1→SOCE is well-supported (C121), though the partial rescue suggests additional mechanisms may contribute. The known localization of Orai1 in caveolae (C87, cited) provides literature support.

results.result: SOCE inhibitors (SKF96365 and CM4620) significantly impair TNBC cell migration and xenograft tumor growth, supporting the EHD2-SOCE axis as a potential therapeutic target in EHD2/CAV1/2-overexpressing breast cancers.
results.evaluation: Two SOCE inhibitors (SKF96365 and CM4620, the latter in clinical trials; C91, C92) significantly reduce wildtype TNBC migration with smaller effects on EHD2-KO cells (C91), supporting SOCE dependence. SKF96365 significantly reduces xenograft tumor growth in vivo (C95). The therapeutic potential (C8, C125, C126) is reasonably supported, though SKF96365 lacks specificity for Orai1 (acknowledged in C124), and more selective inhibitors would strengthen the conclusion. The proposal to use EHD2/CAV1/2 as predictive biomarkers is logical but requires prospective validation.

results.result: The authors' findings of pro-oncogenic EHD2 role contradict prior reports of tumor suppressor function, potentially explained by high adipocyte EHD2 expression confounding bulk tissue analysis and failure to distinguish nuclear vs. cytoplasmic EHD2 in prior studies.
results.evaluation: The proposed explanations for discordance with prior literature (C99) are plausible: high adipocyte EHD2 (C100) could indeed confound bulk tissue western blots, and failure to distinguish subcellular localization (C101) could explain conflicting results given the opposite prognostic associations of nuclear vs. cytoplasmic EHD2. However, these remain speculative explanations (C100, C101 are IMPLICIT claims) without direct experimental validation. The authors appropriately acknowledge antibody validation issues in prior studies, but definitive resolution would require re-analysis of prior datasets or direct comparison experiments.

results.result: Nuclear translocation of EHD2 may sequester it from plasma membrane to inhibit pro-oncogenic SOCE function, potentially explaining opposite prognostic associations of nuclear vs. cytoplasmic EHD2.
results.evaluation: This is explicitly presented as speculation (C106 is IMPLICIT claim with SPECULATION evidence type). While the opposite prognostic associations of nuclear vs. cytoplasmic EHD2 are well-documented (C43, C44), the proposed sequestration mechanism is hypothetical. The authors appropriately state 'rigorous studies will be needed to test this suggestion.' Prior work on EHD2 nuclear shuttling and transcriptional regulation (C102-C105) provides context but not direct support for this specific hypothesis.

results.result: Background knowledge claims establishing context for EHD2 biology, caveolae function, SOCE pathway, and prior cancer studies.
results.evaluation: These claims (C9-C27, C72-C75, C87, C102-C105, C111-C117, C119, C120, C122, C124) are appropriately cited to prior literature and represent established knowledge providing context for the current study. They are not novel findings but necessary background. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are consistent with the field. These establish the rationale for investigating EHD2 in cancer and the SOCE pathway as a potential mechanism.
